paras: The attempted lynching of John Thompson took place on the night of August 11, 1903, at Passyunk square in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, when a crowd of several hundred people chased Thompson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white man, and besieged the trolley car in which he had taken refuge. Firemen from a nearby fire station fought through the crowd and rescued him before police arrived. Southern editors seized on the episode as evidence that Northern cities shared the mob spirit they condemned in the South.

According to the Philadelphia Press, Thompson was said to have knocked down and beaten a white man at 13th and Ellsworth streets, one block north of Passyunk square. The Alexandria Gazette described the alleged attack as an "unprovoked assault upon a white man with a blackjack," and the Baltimore Sun, as summarized in Raleigh, also called it unprovoked. No paper named the white man or reported his injuries.

As Thompson ran, a crowd followed him past the square, where hundreds of people sitting on the benches joined the chase. At Dickinson street he jumped onto a northbound car in 13th street, but the leaders of the pursuit called for others to head it off, and by the time it reached Reed street a dense crowd had blocked the tracks. A dozen men pinned the motorman's arms and shut off the power, others besieged the conductor, and dozens tried to climb through the windows while Thompson crouched behind two women passengers.

The Press put the crowd at "nearly three hundred persons," while the Baltimore Sun's account gave 500 men crying "Lynch him" and "Hang him." The crew of fire truck No. 11, stationed on 12th street below Wharton, left one man with their apparatus, crossed the square in a body armed with whatever they could carry, and pulled Thompson away from a dozen men who already had hold of him. They fought their way back to the fire station and shut the door just before the crowd could storm it.

The police on the beat were elsewhere, and the Snyder avenue station first heard of the trouble when the firemen called for help. Only the arrival of a patrol wagon full of police broke up the crowd, and Thompson was taken to the station in a police wagon.
The coverage reports no arrests among the crowd, and no report of a charge, hearing or trial for Thompson was found.

The fullest account came from the Philadelphia Press, reprinted on August 12 by the Washington Evening Star under the headline "Attempt to Lynch a Negro," which praised the "remarkable bravery" of the firemen and noted that the police had been absent. The story then passed into editorial columns, where it served sectional arguments more than it reported news.

The Alexandria Gazette opened its August 13 paragraph with "People who live in glass houses should not throw stones," setting Philadelphia's outcry against Southern lynching beside the city's own near-lynching. Raleigh's News & Observer, under the heading "Two in One Day," paired it with an attack on Black men in the York area, called Thompson "a bad negro," and argued that Pennsylvanians should stop lecturing the South, while conceding that mob action was wrong in either section.

In Massachusetts, the Worcester Spy wrote on August 14 that the mob's purpose was evidently to make Thompson pay "with his life" and that but for the firemen Philadelphia "might have been disgraced by a lynching." No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.
Accounts differ on the size of the crowd, from nearly 300 in the local Press to 500 in the Baltimore Sun, and on the alleged assault, which only the Gazette said involved a blackjack.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Thompson
bases: A crowd chased and besieged a Black man accused of assaulting a white man in an effort to 'capture and lynch' him, and firemen rescued him before he was killed (A1, A3, A4); it is an attempted lynching.

A crowd of 300 to 500 tried to seize and lynch Thompson over an alleged assault on a white man, acting without any authority (A1, A3), but firemen rescued him and no report says he was killed or seriously hurt (A1, A4); it was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

Two separately sourced reports, the Philadelphia Press reprinted in the Evening Star (A1) and the Baltimore Sun as summarized by the News & Observer (A3), agree on the mob, the alleged assault and the firemen's rescue, and two further editorials repeat the core story (A2, A4).

accounts.label: Philadelphia Press (reprinted in the Evening Star)
accounts.gist: A crowd of nearly 300 stopped a northbound trolley to capture and lynch Thompson after he allegedly beat a white man; the crew of truck No. 11 rescued him while police on the beat were elsewhere.

accounts.label: Baltimore Sun (as summarized by the News & Observer)
accounts.gist: A mob of 500 men crying 'Lynch him' and 'Hang him' tried to seize a 'bad negro' who had made an unprovoked assault on a white man; a whole fire company rescued him and he was taken to the station in a police wagon.

accounts.label: Editorial summaries
accounts.gist: The Alexandria Gazette and the Worcester Spy retold the episode in brief, the Gazette adding that the alleged assault was made with a blackjack.

framing.detail: Headline 'ATTEMPT TO LYNCH A NEGRO. Philadelphia Firemen Rescue Him From Mob Just in Time.', praising the firemen's 'remarkable bravery' while noting the police were elsewhere.
Alexandria Gazette: 'People who live in glass houses should not throw stones'; calls lynched Southern men 'colored brute' and says lynching in the South is condoned 'but for one offense.'

News & Observer, 'Two in One Day': calls Thompson 'a bad negro,' says the episode should teach Pennsylvanians not to lecture the South, but also that mob action 'is wrong, whether displayed in the North or the South.'
Worcester Spy: the mob's purpose was 'to make him pay for his offense with his life'; but for the firemen the city 'might have been disgraced by a lynching.'

conflicts.note: The lower figure comes from the local Philadelphia Press; the higher from the Baltimore Sun as relayed by a Raleigh editorial.
